screens.title: What is UMG and why use it?
screens.narratorSegment: UMG, Unreal Motion Graphics, is the editor and runtime framework you use to build in-game user interfaces. At a minimum, think of it as a designer-friendly environment where widgets—visual building blocks—are arranged into a hierarchical Widget Blueprint that extends UUserWidget. This is distinct from placing objects in the world: a UMG widget is an asset used to render HUDs, menus, and overlays that respond to game state and player input. A concrete example: a health counter is implemented as a Text Block inside a WBP_PlayerHUD. The Visual Designer lets you drag a Canvas Panel, add a Text Block, and bind its text to a health value. Why prefer UMG? Because it provides a consistent, engine-integrated pipeline for authoring, previewing, and scripting UI, and it connects naturally to both Blueprints and C++. One common misconception is that UMG is only for designers; in practice it is a shared toolset—designers craft the visual asset while programmers control instantiation and visibility. A key takeaway: treat Widget Blueprints as assets you can instantiate at runtime, not as static textures, and plan who manages which parts—design or code—to avoid duplicated responsibilities. How will you separate design from runtime control in your next HUD?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: UMG is the visual UI framework where Widget Blueprints define hierarchical widgets that render HUDs, menus, and overlays in-game.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is UMG?
UMG: purpose and role
A visual system to author and render UI assets that connect to game logic.
Core claim
Widget Blueprints are UUserWidget assets. Designers build them in the Designer tab; coders instantiate them at runtime.
Example
Create WBP_PlayerHUD with a Canvas Panel and a Text Block labeled "Health: 100". This is a visual asset you can add to any PlayerController at runtime.
Common misconception
UMG is not limited to designers; it is part of the code/design workflow. Decide which logic lives in Blueprint and which in C++ to avoid duplication.
Key Takeaway

UMG assetizes UI: build visually, control programmatically. That separation keeps iteration fast and code clean.

Widget Blueprint anatomy
Designer tab
Drag widgets from the Palette and arrange them on the Canvas — this determines layout and anchors.
Hierarchy
A tree of widgets that defines nesting and rendering order — like HTML DOM for game UI.
Graph & Details
Blueprint logic lives in Graph; styling and properties are in Details for each widget.
Try this
Open the UMG editor, add a Text Block, change its text to "Player Health: 100" and preview in the Designer to confirm anchors and font size.

screens.title: Create a basic WBP_PlayerHUD
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through creating a simple HUD asset named WBP_PlayerHUD. Begin in the Content Browser: right-click, choose User Interface → Widget Blueprint, select UserWidget as the parent, and name it WBP_PlayerHUD. Open it to see the Designer, Palette, Hierarchy, Details, and Graph panels. First, drag a Canvas Panel from the Palette onto the Designer; this will be your root container and gives you anchors and absolute positioning for key HUD pieces. Next, drag a Text Block into the Canvas Panel and set its Text property to something like "Health: 100" in the Details panel. Use an anchor preset such as top-left so the text keeps a consistent offset across resolutions. Then, drag a Button into the Canvas Panel and place a child Text Block inside it labeled "Menu". Adjust fonts, colors, and padding in Details. Save the Widget Blueprint. A misconception to avoid is overusing the Canvas Panel for everything; reserve it for HUDs needing absolute placement and prefer Horizontal or Vertical Boxes for lists and menus. Finally, preview the widget in the Designer to verify anchors and layout. This process gives you an editable visual asset you can refine before wiring it in C++.

keyIdea.title: Step-by-step
keyIdea.text: Create WBP_PlayerHUD, add a Canvas Panel, add Text Block and Button, anchor them, and preview the layout.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Create WBP_PlayerHUD
Authoring steps
  1. Create Widget Blueprint: Content Browser → User Interface → Widget Blueprint → name WBP_PlayerHUD.
  2. Add Canvas Panel: Drag Canvas Panel into Designer as the root container for the HUD.
  3. Add Text Block: Set text to "Health: 100" and choose top-left anchor preset.
  4. Add Button: Place it in top-right with a child Text Block labeled "Menu".
  5. Adjust styles: Use Details panel for fonts, color, padding; preview in Designer.
Key Takeaway

Follow the Designer flow: asset → root panel → child widgets → anchors → preview. This sequence reduces iteration friction.

Example layout
Canvas Panel use
Best for HUD items needing absolute placement, layered elements, and anchors.
Anchor presets
Use top-left for health counters, top-right for menu buttons, and center for popups that must remain central on any resolution.
Mistake to avoid
Don’t place everything on one Canvas with raw offsets; mixing panel widgets improves responsiveness.

screens.title: Panel widgets: when to use each
screens.narratorSegment: Panel widgets are the containers that determine how child widgets are positioned and scaled. Choosing the right panel is crucial for responsive UI. Canvas Panel gives you anchors and offsets for absolute or layered HUD elements; use it for fixed-position overlays like health counters or crosshairs. Horizontal Box arranges children horizontally — ideal for status bars, grouped icons, and side-by-side counts. Vertical Box stacks children vertically; it's the natural choice for menus and inventory lists. Grid Panel places children into rows and columns when you need structured grids. Overlay stacks widgets on top of each other, useful for pop-ups or layered visual effects. Size Box enforces specific dimensions on a single child and is useful when a widget must maintain an exact size regardless of parent layout. A common misconception is that Canvas Panel is always simpler; in reality, misusing it for complex, variable-length content often causes poor scaling. In practice combine panels: use a Canvas for the HUD root, then a Horizontal Box inside it for grouped elements so your UI adapts without manual repositioning. Which panel will you pick for your next menu?

keyIdea.text: Pick panels based on layout needs: Canvas for HUD anchors, Horizontal/Vertical for lists, Grid for tables, Overlay for stacking, and Size Box for fixed sizing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Panel widgets
Panel Types
Canvas Panel
Anchors + offsets for absolute placement and layering — great for HUDs and fixed overlays.
Horizontal Box
Auto-arranges children horizontally. Use Fill or Auto sizing for flexible groups like status bars.
Vertical Box
Stacks children vertically; ideal for menus, settings, and inventory lists.
More panels
Grid Panel
Lay out widgets in rows and columns for structured interfaces like inventory grids.
Overlay
Stack widgets on top of each other, useful for pop-ups, fade layers, and effects.
Size Box
Force a specific width/height for a child, handy for icons and fixed controls within flexible layouts.
Common mistake
Relying on Canvas for everything leads to brittle UIs. Mix panels to gain adaptability.

screens.title: Key widget types: Text Block, Image, Button
screens.narratorSegment: Text Blocks, Images, and Buttons are the foundational visible widgets you will use in most HUDs and menus. A Text Block renders formatted text and supports font size, color, and wrapping; use it for labels like "Health: 100". An Image displays a texture or brush and is commonly used for icons, portraits, or decorative bars. A Button is an interactive widget that can contain other widgets, typically a child Text Block for its label. Configure Button events in the Graph or from C++ by binding delegates. A concrete example: create a button anchored to the top-right labeled "Menu" with a child Text Block, then style the Button's Normal and Hovered colors in Details for visual feedback. Misconceptions include expecting Buttons to be interactive without input mode changes; ensure your PlayerController or HUD does not block UI input and that the widget is focusable when necessary. Finally, remember that images and text can be data-bound: you often change a Text Block's content or an Image's brush in Construct rather than Tick to avoid per-frame overhead. How will you structure the health display to update only when values change?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Widget types
Basic elements explained
Text Block
Used for labels, values, and rich text. Configure font, color, alignment, and wrapping in Details.
Image
Shows a texture or brush. Useful for icons, portraits, or decoration; use Size Box to control dimensions.
Button
Interactive container. Place a Text Block inside, style states (Normal/Hovered/Pressed), and connect events in Graph.
Practical tip
Update Text Block values in response to events or bindings, not every frame. Use Construct or event-driven updates.
Concrete example
Health + Menu
Text Block: "Health: 100" anchored top-left. Button with child Text Block: "Menu" anchored top-right. Style hover colors and test click events in Graph.
Mistake
Assuming Buttons work without input handling; ensure your PlayerController allows UI input and the widget is focusable if you expect keyboard/controller navigation.

screens.title: Instantiate and show a widget from C++
screens.narratorSegment: To show your WBP_PlayerHUD at runtime you create an instance of the widget class and add it to the viewport. In C++ this pattern uses CreateWidget and AddToViewport on a UUserWidget pointer. Concretely, add a TSubclassOf PlayerHUDClass property to your AMyPlayerController header and a UUserWidget* PlayerHUD instance pointer. Call CreateWidget (this, PlayerHUDClass) to create the widget and then PlayerHUD->AddToViewport() to render it. If PlayerHUDClass is unset, log an error and avoid calling CreateWidget. Common practice is to call this logic from BeginPlay so the HUD appears when the player spawns. One misconception is to assume CreateWidget automatically adds a widget to the screen; it only constructs the object — AddToViewport is required to make it visible. Another key point is lifecycle: you can cache the instance and call RemoveFromParent() to hide it, or set visibility to Collapsed to keep it in memory. This pattern cleanly separates asset selection in Blueprints from runtime logic in C++. Instantiate and show a widget from C++ means use tsubclassof to reference the widget blueprint class, createwidget to instantiate, and addtoviewport to show the widget; removefromparent or setvisibility to hide it.. In practical terms, createwidget and addtoviewport pattern in amyplayercontroller. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › C++: CreateWidget & AddToViewport
Starter code
// In AMyPlayerController.h
protected:
	UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "UI")
	TSubclassOf<UUserWidget> PlayerHUDClass;

	UPROPERTY()
	UUserWidget* PlayerHUD;

	void CreateAndAddPlayerHUD();

// In AMyPlayerController.cpp
#include "Blueprint/UserWidget.h"

void AMyPlayerController::BeginPlay()
{
	Super::BeginPlay();
	CreateAndAddPlayerHUD();
}

void AMyPlayerController::CreateAndAddPlayerHUD()
{
	if (PlayerHUDClass)
	{
		PlayerHUD = CreateWidget<UUserWidget>(this, PlayerHUDClass);
		if (PlayerHUD)
		{
			PlayerHUD->AddToViewport();
			UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Player HUD created and added to viewport."));
		}
	}
	else
	{
		UE_LOG(LogTemp, Error, TEXT("PlayerHUDClass is not set in MyPlayerController!"));
	}
}
Runtime notes
CreateWidget constructs the widget; AddToViewport displays it. Use RemoveFromParent or SetVisibility to hide it later.
Example scenario
Game start HUD
Set PlayerHUDClass in BP_MyPlayerController to WBP_PlayerHUD and confirm the log message when BeginPlay runs in Play in Editor.
Mistake to avoid
Forgetting to set PlayerHUDClass in a Blueprint subclass results in no widget being created even if the code is correct.

screens.title: Blueprint setup and GameMode wiring
screens.narratorSegment: After you implement PlayerHUDClass and the creation function in C++, the next step is a small Blueprint configuration. Create a Blueprint subclass of your AMyPlayerController, for example BP_MyPlayerController. In the Details panel, set the PlayerHUDClass variable to your WBP_PlayerHUD asset. This lets designers assign specific Widget Blueprints without recompiling C++ code. Then open your project's GameMode Blueprint and set the Player Controller Class to BP_MyPlayerController. This wiring ensures that when the game starts the engine spawns your controller class, BeginPlay calls CreateAndAddPlayerHUD, and the widget appears on screen. A common misconception is to forget to update GameMode; even if your controller Blueprint is correct, the engine must be configured to use it. For testing, run Play in Editor and check the output log for the "Player HUD created and added to viewport" message. If you see an error that PlayerHUDClass is not set, open BP_MyPlayerController and assign the widget asset. This small handshake between Blueprints and C++ gives you flexible asset assignment and predictable runtime behavior. Blueprint setup and GameMode wiring means assign the widget blueprint class in a bp_myplayercontroller and set that controller as the player controller class in your gamemode to spawn the hud at beginplay.. In practical terms, bp_myplayercontroller and gamemode configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Widget lifecycle and performance
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the lifecycle of a UUserWidget helps you place initialization and cleanup code correctly. Construct runs when a widget is first created and is the appropriate place to set up bindings, initialize values, or hook into events. Tick, if enabled, runs every frame and should be used sparingly — expensive work in Tick can degrade both UI and game performance. Destruct is invoked when a widget is removed and is where you remove listeners or free resources. For example, bind a delegate to a health-change event in Construct and update the Text Block only when that event fires; do not poll the player’s health in Tick. A frequent misconception is to expect Construct to run only once per game; it runs when the widget is constructed, which could happen multiple times if you create and destroy the widget repeatedly. To avoid unnecessary reconstructions, consider caching the widget instance or toggling visibility. The core takeaway: initialize in Construct, respond to events, avoid heavy Tick work, and clean up in Destruct to keep your UI efficient and predictable. Widget lifecycle and performance means use construct to initialize, avoid per-frame work in tick, and clean up in destruct; prefer event-driven updates for performance.. In practical terms, construct, tick, and destruct explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Troubleshooting and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: When building UMG UIs you'll encounter a few recurring pitfalls. First, forgetting to call AddToViewport after CreateWidget results in a valid widget instance that never appears; the code compiles but the screen stays blank. Second, not assigning PlayerHUDClass in a Blueprint subclass means CreateWidget receives a null class and nothing is created; always set the variable in BP_MyPlayerController or use ConstructorHelpers::FClassFinder if you prefer a C++ default. Third, over-relying on Canvas Panel and hard-coded offsets yields UIs that break across resolutions; use Horizontal Box, Vertical Box, or Grid for responsive areas. Fourth, doing heavy work in Tick for updating visuals can harm performance; instead bind to events and update only when values change. A recommended debugging sequence is: confirm PlayerHUDClass is set, check GameMode uses your controller, run Play and watch the log for the debug message, and then inspect the Designer anchors. These steps resolve most "missing HUD" issues and keep your UI maintainable and performant. In practical terms, avoiding missing widgets, poor scaling, and performance problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Assessment example: toggle an inventory screen
screens.narratorSegment: A practical assessment is to implement toggling an inventory screen when the player presses a key. The C++ approach begins with two properties in your PlayerController: a TSubclassOf<UUserWidget> InventoryWidgetClass and a UUserWidget* InventoryWidgetInstance. On the first key press, if InventoryWidgetInstance is null, call CreateWidget<UUserWidget>(this, InventoryWidgetClass) to create it and then AddToViewport to display it. Set a boolean flag like bIsInventoryOpen to track state. When the key is pressed again, check the widget instance: if it is visible, call RemoveFromParent() or SetVisibility to hide it and update the flag. If you prefer to keep the widget in memory, use SetVisibility(ESlateVisibility::Collapsed), which prevents reallocation but still uses memory. The key learning points are managing the widget instance lifecycle and deciding between remove/create versus toggle visibility for performance. A common mistake is creating a new instance on every open without removing or storing references, which can leak memory or produce duplicate widgets. How will you balance memory use against creation overhead in your game? fullNarratorScript:
UMG is Unreal Engine's visual UI system for creating in-game interfaces that communicate with players and respond to game state. In this lesson you will see why UMG matters, how Widget Blueprints are the primary assets for UI, and how C++ and Blueprints work together to display HUD elements like health counters and menus. You will also get a practical path: create a WBP_PlayerHUD, add Text Blocks and Buttons, and instantiate it from your PlayerController using CreateWidget and AddToViewport. As you follow along, observe that widgets are hierarchical assets: a root panel contains children, and panel widgets control layout and responsiveness. This matters because a stable layout keeps your UI readable across resolutions; relying solely on absolute positioning often breaks across screens. We'll cover the typical UMG panels — Canvas, Horizontal Box, Vertical Box — and show common lifecycle events like Construct and Tick so you can manage performance. By the end you'll have a simple HUD in the editor and the steps to wire it from C++, giving you a foundation for more complex menus and HUDs. Think about one UI you use in a game; this lesson shows how you would build and show it using UMG.

By the end of these first steps you will understand UMG's purpose and its core pieces. First, you'll be able to explain why UMG is the right system for in-game UI and identify the main panels and widget types you use to build a HUD. Second, you will create a basic Widget Blueprint and learn to add Text Blocks, Images, and Buttons inside a Canvas Panel. Third, you'll design simple layouts using Horizontal and Vertical Boxes so your UI adapts better to different resolutions instead of relying on fixed coordinates. Fourth, you will wire a Widget Blueprint into your PlayerController so that the HUD appears when the game starts. Each objective pairs a practical skill with an explanation of why it matters: responsive layout keeps UIs readable across devices and instantiating widgets from C++ lets gameplay code control visibility, input, and lifecycle. As you work, think about the difference between visual design in the Designer tab and runtime control from C++—both are essential. We'll soon walk through a hands-on lab to create WBP_PlayerHUD, set PlayerHUDClass, and validate the widget appears in the viewport.

These objectives focus on practice and lifecycle awareness so your UI works correctly at runtime. You will establish how widgets are structured and rendered, recognizing the hierarchy that connects a root panel to nested children. You will create a concrete WBP_PlayerHUD and test it in the editor so you can iterate on visual design and anchors until it scales. You will configure a BP_MyPlayerController and set PlayerHUDClass so gameplay code can instantiate the widget class. Finally, you will learn the key lifecycle events: Construct, Tick, and Destruct, and why avoiding expensive per-frame work in Tick matters for performance. Each item pairs a task and a rationale: for example, Construct is the place to initialize bindings while Tick should rarely perform heavy logic; that keeps your UI and game running smoothly. These objectives prepare you to complete the hands-on activity that creates the HUD, wires it in C++, and tests it during Play in Editor. Keep these aims in mind as checkpoints while you work.

UMG, Unreal Motion Graphics, is the editor and runtime framework you use to build in-game user interfaces. At a minimum, think of it as a designer-friendly environment where widgets—visual building blocks—are arranged into a hierarchical Widget Blueprint that extends UUserWidget. This is distinct from placing objects in the world: a UMG widget is an asset used to render HUDs, menus, and overlays that respond to game state and player input. A concrete example: a health counter is implemented as a Text Block inside a WBP_PlayerHUD. The Visual Designer lets you drag a Canvas Panel, add a Text Block, and bind its text to a health value. Why prefer UMG? Because it provides a consistent, engine-integrated pipeline for authoring, previewing, and scripting UI, and it connects naturally to both Blueprints and C++. One common misconception is that UMG is only for designers; in practice it is a shared toolset—designers craft the visual asset while programmers control instantiation and visibility. A key takeaway: treat Widget Blueprints as assets you can instantiate at runtime, not as static textures, and plan who manages which parts—design or code—to avoid duplicated responsibilities. How will you separate design from runtime control in your next HUD?

Let's walk through creating a simple HUD asset named WBP_PlayerHUD. Begin in the Content Browser: right-click, choose User Interface → Widget Blueprint, select UserWidget as the parent, and name it WBP_PlayerHUD. Open it to see the Designer, Palette, Hierarchy, Details, and Graph panels. First, drag a Canvas Panel from the Palette onto the Designer; this will be your root container and gives you anchors and absolute positioning for key HUD pieces. Next, drag a Text Block into the Canvas Panel and set its Text property to something like "Health: 100" in the Details panel. Use an anchor preset such as top-left so the text keeps a consistent offset across resolutions. Then, drag a Button into the Canvas Panel and place a child Text Block inside it labeled "Menu". Adjust fonts, colors, and padding in Details. Save the Widget Blueprint. A misconception to avoid is overusing the Canvas Panel for everything; reserve it for HUDs needing absolute placement and prefer Horizontal or Vertical Boxes for lists and menus. Finally, preview the widget in the Designer to verify anchors and layout. This process gives you an editable visual asset you can refine before wiring it in C++.

Panel widgets are the containers that determine how child widgets are positioned and scaled. Choosing the right panel is crucial for responsive UI. Canvas Panel gives you anchors and offsets for absolute or layered HUD elements; use it for fixed-position overlays like health counters or crosshairs. Horizontal Box arranges children horizontally — ideal for status bars, grouped icons, and side-by-side counts. Vertical Box stacks children vertically; it's the natural choice for menus and inventory lists. Grid Panel places children into rows and columns when you need structured grids. Overlay stacks widgets on top of each other, useful for pop-ups or layered visual effects. Size Box enforces specific dimensions on a single child and is useful when a widget must maintain an exact size regardless of parent layout. A common misconception is that Canvas Panel is always simpler; in reality, misusing it for complex, variable-length content often causes poor scaling. In practice combine panels: use a Canvas for the HUD root, then a Horizontal Box inside it for grouped elements so your UI adapts without manual repositioning. Which panel will you pick for your next menu?

Text Blocks, Images, and Buttons are the foundational visible widgets you will use in most HUDs and menus. A Text Block renders formatted text and supports font size, color, and wrapping; use it for labels like "Health: 100". An Image displays a texture or brush and is commonly used for icons, portraits, or decorative bars. A Button is an interactive widget that can contain other widgets, typically a child Text Block for its label. Configure Button events in the Graph or from C++ by binding delegates. A concrete example: create a button anchored to the top-right labeled "Menu" with a child Text Block, then style the Button's Normal and Hovered colors in Details for visual feedback. Misconceptions include expecting Buttons to be interactive without input mode changes; ensure your PlayerController or HUD does not block UI input and that the widget is focusable when necessary. Finally, remember that images and text can be data-bound: you often change a Text Block's content or an Image's brush in Construct rather than Tick to avoid per-frame overhead. How will you structure the health display to update only when values change?

To show your WBP_PlayerHUD at runtime you create an instance of the widget class and add it to the viewport. In C++ this pattern uses CreateWidget and AddToViewport on a UUserWidget pointer. Concretely, add a TSubclassOf PlayerHUDClass property to your AMyPlayerController header and a UUserWidget* PlayerHUD instance pointer. Call CreateWidget (this, PlayerHUDClass) to create the widget and then PlayerHUD->AddToViewport() to render it. If PlayerHUDClass is unset, log an error and avoid calling CreateWidget. Common practice is to call this logic from BeginPlay so the HUD appears when the player spawns. One misconception is to assume CreateWidget automatically adds a widget to the screen; it only constructs the object — AddToViewport is required to make it visible. Another key point is lifecycle: you can cache the instance and call RemoveFromParent() to hide it, or set visibility to Collapsed to keep it in memory. This pattern cleanly separates asset selection in Blueprints from runtime logic in C++. Instantiate and show a widget from C++ means use tsubclassof to reference the widget blueprint class, createwidget to instantiate, and addtoviewport to show the widget; removefromparent or setvisibility to hide it.. Understanding the lifecycle of a UUserWidget helps you place initialization and cleanup code correctly. Construct runs when a widget is first created and is the appropriate place to set up bindings, initialize values, or hook into events. Tick, if enabled, runs every frame and should be used sparingly — expensive work in Tick can degrade both UI and game performance. Destruct is invoked when a widget is removed and is where you remove listeners or free resources. For example, bind a delegate to a health-change event in Construct and update the Text Block only when that event fires; do not poll the player’s health in Tick. A frequent misconception is to expect Construct to run only once per game; it runs when the widget is constructed, which could happen multiple times if you create and destroy the widget repeatedly. To avoid unnecessary reconstructions, consider caching the widget instance or toggling visibility. The core takeaway: initialize in Construct, respond to events, avoid heavy Tick work, and clean up in Destruct to keep your UI efficient and predictable. When building UMG UIs you'll encounter a few recurring pitfalls. First, forgetting to call AddToViewport after CreateWidget results in a valid widget instance that never appears; the code compiles but the screen stays blank. Second, not assigning PlayerHUDClass in a Blueprint subclass means CreateWidget receives a null class and nothing is created; always set the variable in BP_MyPlayerController or use ConstructorHelpers::FClassFinder if you prefer a C++ default. Third, over-relying on Canvas Panel and hard-coded offsets yields UIs that break across resolutions; use Horizontal Box, Vertical Box, or Grid for responsive areas. Fourth, doing heavy work in Tick for updating visuals can harm performance; instead bind to events and update only when values change. A recommended debugging sequence is: confirm PlayerHUDClass is set, check GameMode uses your controller, run Play and watch the log for the debug message, and then inspect the Designer anchors.
